drug_class: Chemotherapy agent (topoisomerase II inhibitor / podophyllotoxin derivative)
purpose: Etoposide is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain types of cancer, including lung cancer and testicular cancer. It may be used alone or combined with other cancer medicines. Your doctor may also use it for other cancers not listed here.
how_it_works: Cancer cells grow by making copies of themselves, which requires them to unwind and copy their DNA. Etoposide blocks a special protein that cancer cells need to do this, causing the DNA to break and preventing the cancer cell from dividing and growing. This helps slow down or stop the spread of cancer in your body.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite are very common. You may notice hair loss, mouth sores, diarrhea, and feeling very tired or weak. Your blood counts will likely drop, which can make you more prone to infections, bruising, or bleeding. Low blood pressure can happen during IV infusions.
warnings: Because this medicine lowers your white blood cell count, you are at a higher risk of serious infections — contact your doctor right away if you have a fever, chills, or signs of infection. It can also lower platelets and red blood cells, increasing risk of bleeding and anemia. Etoposide can cause serious birth defects, so do not get pregnant or father a child during treatment. There is also a small long-term risk of developing a second type of cancer called leukemia. Always tell your care team about all other medicines you take.
typical_dosing: The dose depends on your type of cancer, your body size, kidney and liver function, and what other medicines you are taking. It is usually given as an IV infusion in a clinic or hospital over 30 to 60 minutes, or sometimes as a capsule taken by mouth. Your oncology team will calculate the exact dose and schedule that is right for you — never adjust it on your own.
